# typewit/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)#![allow(clippy::needless_doctest_main)]
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! This crate provides abstractions for creating
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! [type witnesses](#what-are-type-witnesses).
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//!
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! The inciting motivation for this crate is emulating trait polymorphism in `const fn`
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! (as of 2025-07-20, it's not possible to call trait methods in const contexts on stable).
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//!
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! # What are type witnesses
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! Type witnesses are values that prove the equality of a type parameter to a
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! fixed set of possible types.
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! The simplest type witness is [`TypeEq<L, R>`][`TypeEq`],
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! which only proves equality of its `L` and `R` type parameters,
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! and can be used to coerce between them.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! Most type witnesses are enums with [`TypeEq`] fields,
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! which can coerce between a type parameter and as many types as there are variants.
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! # Examples
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! <span id="example0"></span>
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! ### Polymorphic function
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! This demonstrates how one can write a polymorphic `const fn`
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! (as of 2025-07-20, trait methods can't be called in const fns on stable)
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! (this example requires Rust 1.61.0, since it uses trait bounds in const)
[30](https://docs.rs#30)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "rust_1_61"), doc = "```ignore")]
[31](https://docs.rs#31)#![cfg_attr(feature = "rust_1_61", doc = "```rust")]
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! use typewit::{HasTypeWitness, TypeEq};
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! const VALS: [&str; 6] = [
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!     message(0),
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!     message(1),
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!     message(2),
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!     message(3),
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!     message("hi"),
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!     message("foo"),
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! ];
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! assert_eq!(VALS, ["A", "B", "C", "A", "hi", "foo"]);
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! // A "method" of the `Message` trait (declared below)
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! const fn message<'a, T: Message<'a>>(val: T) -> &'a str {
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!     match HasTypeWitness::WITNESS {
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!         MessageWitness::Usize(te) => {
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!             // `te` (a `TypeEq<T, usize>`) allows coercing between `T` and `usize`,
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!             // because `TypeEq` is a value-level proof that both types are the same.
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!             let index: usize = te.to_right(val);
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!             ["A", "B", "C"][index % 3]
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//!         }
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!         MessageWitness::Str(te) => {
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//!             // `te` is a `TypeEq<T, &'a str>`
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!             te.to_right(val)
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//!         }
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!     }
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! }
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! // The trait that we use to emulate polymorphic dispatch,
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! // the limitation is that it can only emulate it for a limited set of types known
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! // to the crate that defines the trait, in this case that's `usize` and `&str`.
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! trait Message<'a>: HasTypeWitness<MessageWitness<'a, Self>> { }
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! // replacing these impls with a blanket impl leads to worse compilation errors
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! impl<'a> Message<'a> for usize {}
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! impl<'a> Message<'a> for &'a str {}
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! // This macro declares `enum MessageWitness<'a, __Wit>`, a type witness enum,
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! // where each variant requires and then guarantees `__Wit` to be a particular type.
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! // (the `__Wit` type parameter is implicitly added after all generics)
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//! typewit::simple_type_witness! {
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!     enum MessageWitness<'a> {
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!         // This variant requires `__Wit == usize`
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!         Usize = usize,
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!         // This variant requires `__Wit == &'a str`
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!         Str = &'a str,
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!     }
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! }
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! ```
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! <span id="example-uses-type-fn"></span>
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! ### Indexing polymorphism
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! This function demonstrates const fn polymorphism
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! and projecting [`TypeEq`] by implementing [`TypeFn`].
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//!
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! (this example requires Rust 1.71.0, because it uses `<[T]>::split_at` in a const context.
[91](https://docs.rs#91)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "rust_stable"), doc = "```ignore")]
[92](https://docs.rs#92)#![cfg_attr(feature = "rust_stable", doc = "```rust")]
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! use std::ops::Range;
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! use typewit::{HasTypeWitness, TypeEq};
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! fn main() {
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!     let array = [3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55, 89];
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!     assert_eq!(index(&array, 0), &3);
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!     assert_eq!(index(&array, 3), &13);
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//!     assert_eq!(index(&array, 0..4), [3, 5, 8, 13]);
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//!     assert_eq!(index(&array, 3..5), [13, 21]);
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! }
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//!
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! const fn index<T, I>(slice: &[T], idx: I) -> &SliceIndexRet<I, T>
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! where
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!     I: SliceIndex<T>,
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! {
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!     // `I::WITNESS` is `<I as HasTypeWitness<IndexWitness<I>>>::WITNESS`,
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!     match I::WITNESS {
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!         IndexWitness::Usize(arg_te) => {
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!             // `arg_te` (a `TypeEq<I, usize>`) allows coercing between `I` and `usize`,
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!             // because `TypeEq` is a value-level proof that both types are the same.
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//!             let idx: usize = arg_te.to_right(idx);
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!             // using the `TypeFn` impl for `FnSliceIndexRet<T>` to
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!             // map `TypeEq<I, usize>`
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!             // to  `TypeEq<SliceIndexRet<I, T>, SliceIndexRet<usize, T>>`
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!             arg_te.project::<FnSliceIndexRet<T>>()
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!                 // converts`TypeEq<SliceIndexRet<I, T>, T>`
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!                 //      to `TypeEq<&SliceIndexRet<I, T>, &T>`
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!                 .in_ref()
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!                 .to_left(&slice[idx])
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!         }
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!         IndexWitness::Range(arg_te) => {
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!             let range: Range<usize> = arg_te.to_right(idx);
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//!             let ret: &[T] = slice_range(slice, range);
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!             arg_te.project::<FnSliceIndexRet<T>>().in_ref().to_left(ret)
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//!         }
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!     }
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! }
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! // This macro declares a type witness enum
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! typewit::simple_type_witness! {
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!     // Declares `enum IndexWitness<__Wit>`
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!     // (the `__Wit` type parameter is implicitly added after all generics)
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//!     enum IndexWitness {
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!         // This variant requires `__Wit == usize`
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!         Usize = usize,
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!         // This variant requires `__Wit == Range<usize>`
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!         Range = Range<usize>,
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!     }
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! }
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//!
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! /// Trait for all types that can be used as slice indices
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! ///
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! /// The `HasTypeWitness` supertrait allows getting a `IndexWitness<Self>`
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! /// with its `WITNESS` associated constant.
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! trait SliceIndex<T>: HasTypeWitness<IndexWitness<Self>> + Sized {
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!     type Returns: ?Sized;
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! }
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! impl<T> SliceIndex<T> for usize {
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!     type Returns = T;
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! }
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! impl<T> SliceIndex<T> for Range<usize> {
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!     type Returns = [T];
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! }
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! type SliceIndexRet<I, T> = <I as SliceIndex<T>>::Returns;
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! // Declares `struct FnSliceIndexRet<T>`
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! // a type-level function (TypeFn implementor) from `I` to `SliceIndexRet<I, T>`
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! typewit::type_fn! {
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!     struct FnSliceIndexRet<T>;
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//!
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!     impl<I: SliceIndex<T>> I => SliceIndexRet<I, T>
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! }
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//!
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! const fn slice_range<T>(slice: &[T], range: Range<usize>) -> &[T] {
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//!     let suffix = slice.split_at(range.start).1;
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//!     suffix.split_at(range.end - range.start).0
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! }
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//!
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! ```
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//!
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! When the wrong type is passed for the index,
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//! the compile-time error is the same as with normal generic functions:
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! ```text
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! error[E0277]: the trait bound `RangeFull: SliceIndex<{integer}>` is not satisfied
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//!   --> src/main.rs:43:30
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//!    |
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! 13 |     assert_eq!(index(&array, ..), [13, 21]);
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//!    |                -----         ^^ the trait `SliceIndex<{integer}>` is not implemented for `RangeFull`
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//!    |                |
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//!    |                required by a bound introduced by this call
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//!    |
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//!    = help: the following other types implement trait `SliceIndex<T>`:
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//!              std::ops::Range<usize>
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//!              usize
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! ```
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//!
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! ### Downcasting const generic type
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//!
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! This example demonstrates "downcasting" from a type with a const parameter to
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! a concrete instance of that type.
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//!
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! ```rust
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! use typewit::{const_marker::Usize, TypeCmp, TypeEq};
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//!
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//! assert_eq!(*mutate(&mut Arr([])), Arr([]));
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! assert_eq!(*mutate(&mut Arr([1])), Arr([1]));
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! assert_eq!(*mutate(&mut Arr([1, 2])), Arr([1, 2]));
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//! assert_eq!(*mutate(&mut Arr([1, 2, 3])), Arr([1, 3, 6])); // this is different!
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! assert_eq!(*mutate(&mut Arr([1, 2, 3, 4])), Arr([1, 2, 3, 4]));
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//!
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! #[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! struct Arr<const N: usize>([u8; N]);
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//!
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! fn mutate<const N: usize>(arr: &mut Arr<N>) -> &mut Arr<N> {
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//!     if let TypeCmp::Eq(te) =  Usize::<N>.equals(Usize::<3>) {
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//!         let tem = te // `te` is a `TypeEq<Usize<N>, Usize<3>>`
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//!             .project::<GArr>() // returns `TypeEq<Arr<N>, Arr<3>>`
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//!             .in_mut(); // returns `TypeEq<&mut Arr<N>, &mut Arr<3>>`
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//!
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//!         // `tem.to_right(arr)` downcasts `arr` to `&mut Arr<3>`
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//!         tetra_sum(tem.to_right(arr));
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//!     }
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//!
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//!     arr
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! }
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//!
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! fn tetra_sum(arr: &mut Arr<3>) {
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//!     arr.0[1] += arr.0[0];
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//!     arr.0[2] += arr.0[1];
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//! }
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//!
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! // Declares `struct GArr`
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! // a type-level function (TypeFn implementor) from `Usize<N>` to `Arr<N>`
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! typewit::type_fn!{
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//!     struct GArr;
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//!
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//!     impl<const N: usize> Usize<N> => Arr<N>
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//! }
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//! ```
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//!
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! ### Builder
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//!
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//! Using a type witness to help encode a type-level enum,
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//! and to match on that type-level enum inside of a function.
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//!
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//! The type-level enum is used to track the initialization of fields in a builder.
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//!
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! This example requires Rust 1.65.0, because it uses Generic Associated Types.
[246](https://docs.rs#246)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "rust_1_65"), doc = "```ignore")]
[247](https://docs.rs#247)#![cfg_attr(feature = "rust_1_65", doc = "```rust")]
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! use typewit::HasTypeWitness;
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//!
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! fn main() {
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//!     // all default fields
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//!     assert_eq!(
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//!         StructBuilder::new().build(),
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//!         Struct{foo: "default value".into(), bar: vec![3, 5, 8]},
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//!     );
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//!
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//!     // defaulted bar field
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!     assert_eq!(
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//!         StructBuilder::new().foo("hello").build(),
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//!         Struct{foo: "hello".into(), bar: vec![3, 5, 8]},
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//!     );
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//!
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//!     // defaulted foo field
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//!     assert_eq!(
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//!         StructBuilder::new().bar([13, 21, 34]).build(),
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//!         Struct{foo: "default value".into(), bar: vec![13, 21, 34]},
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//!     );
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//!
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//!     // all initialized fields
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//!     assert_eq!(
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//!         StructBuilder::new().foo("world").bar([55, 89]).build(),
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//!         Struct{foo: "world".into(), bar: vec![55, 89]},
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//!     );
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! }
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//!
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//!
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//! #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//! struct Struct {
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//!     foo: String,
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//!     bar: Vec<u32>,
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//! }
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//!
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//! struct StructBuilder<FooInit: InitState, BarInit: InitState> {
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//!     // If `FooInit` is `Uninit`, then this field is a `()`
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//!     // If `FooInit` is `Init`, then this field is a `String`
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//!     foo: BuilderField<FooInit, String>,
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//!
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//!     // If `BarInit` is `Uninit`, then this field is a `()`
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//!     // If `BarInit` is `Init`, then this field is a `Vec<u32>`
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//!     bar: BuilderField<BarInit, Vec<u32>>,
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//! }
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//!
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//! impl StructBuilder<Uninit, Uninit> {
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//!     pub const fn new() -> Self {
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//!         Self {
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//!             foo: (),
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//!             bar: (),
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//!         }
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//!     }
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//! }
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//!
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//! impl<FooInit: InitState, BarInit: InitState> StructBuilder<FooInit, BarInit> {
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//!     /// Sets the `foo` field
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//!     pub fn foo(self, foo: impl Into<String>) -> StructBuilder<Init, BarInit> {
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//!         StructBuilder {
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//!             foo: foo.into(),
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//!             bar: self.bar,
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//!         }
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//!     }
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//!
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//!     /// Sets the `bar` field
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//!     pub fn bar(self, bar: impl Into<Vec<u32>>) -> StructBuilder<FooInit, Init> {
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//!         StructBuilder {
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//!             foo: self.foo,
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//!             bar: bar.into(),
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//!         }
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//!     }
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//!
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//!     /// Builds `Struct`,
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//!     /// providing default values for fields that haven't been set.
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//!     pub fn build(self) -> Struct {
[322](https://docs.rs#322)//!         Struct {
[323](https://docs.rs#323)//!             foo: init_or_else::<FooInit, _, _>(self.foo, || "default value".to_string()),
[324](https://docs.rs#324)//!             bar: init_or_else::<BarInit, _, _>(self.bar, || vec![3, 5, 8]),
[325](https://docs.rs#325)//!         }
[326](https://docs.rs#326)//!     }
[327](https://docs.rs#327)//! }
[328](https://docs.rs#328)//!
[329](https://docs.rs#329)//! // Emulates a type-level `enum InitState { Init, Uninit }`
[330](https://docs.rs#330)//! trait InitState: Sized + HasTypeWitness<InitWit<Self>> {
[331](https://docs.rs#331)//!     // How a builder represents an initialized/uninitialized field.
[332](https://docs.rs#332)//!     // If `Self` is `Uninit`, then this is `()`.
[333](https://docs.rs#333)//!     // If `Self` is `Init`, then this is `T`.
[334](https://docs.rs#334)//!     type BuilderField<T>;
[335](https://docs.rs#335)//! }
[336](https://docs.rs#336)//!
[337](https://docs.rs#337)//! // If `I` is `Uninit`, then this evaluates to `()`
[338](https://docs.rs#338)//! // If `I` is `Init`, then this evaluates to `T`
[339](https://docs.rs#339)//! type BuilderField<I, T> = <I as InitState>::BuilderField::<T>;
[340](https://docs.rs#340)//!
[341](https://docs.rs#341)//! /// Gets `T` out of `maybe_init` if it's actually initialized,
[342](https://docs.rs#342)//! /// otherwise returns `else_()`.
[343](https://docs.rs#343)//! fn init_or_else<I, T, F>(maybe_init: BuilderField<I, T>, else_: F) -> T
[344](https://docs.rs#344)//! where
[345](https://docs.rs#345)//!     I: InitState,
[346](https://docs.rs#346)//!     F: FnOnce() -> T
[347](https://docs.rs#347)//! {
[348](https://docs.rs#348)//!     typewit::type_fn! {
[349](https://docs.rs#349)//!         // Declares the `HelperFn` type-level function (TypeFn implementor)
[350](https://docs.rs#350)//!         // from `I` to `BuilderField<I, T>`
[351](https://docs.rs#351)//!         struct HelperFn<T>;
[352](https://docs.rs#352)//!         impl<I: InitState> I => BuilderField<I, T>
[353](https://docs.rs#353)//!     }
[354](https://docs.rs#354)//!
[355](https://docs.rs#355)//!     // matching on the type-level `InitState` enum by using `InitWit`.
[356](https://docs.rs#356)//!     // `WITNESS` comes from the `HasTypeWitness` trait
[357](https://docs.rs#357)//!     match I::WITNESS {
[358](https://docs.rs#358)//!         // `te: TypeEq<FooInit, Init>`
[359](https://docs.rs#359)//!         InitWit::InitW(te) => {
[360](https://docs.rs#360)//!             te.map(HelperFn::NEW) //: TypeEq<BuilderField<I, T>, T>
[361](https://docs.rs#361)//!               .to_right(maybe_init)
[362](https://docs.rs#362)//!         }
[363](https://docs.rs#363)//!         InitWit::UninitW(_) => else_(),
[364](https://docs.rs#364)//!     }
[365](https://docs.rs#365)//! }
[366](https://docs.rs#366)//!
[367](https://docs.rs#367)//! // Emulates a type-level `InitState::Init` variant.
[368](https://docs.rs#368)//! // Marks a field as initialized.
[369](https://docs.rs#369)//! enum Init {}
[370](https://docs.rs#370)//!
[371](https://docs.rs#371)//! impl InitState for Init {
[372](https://docs.rs#372)//!     type BuilderField<T> = T;
[373](https://docs.rs#373)//! }
[374](https://docs.rs#374)//!
[375](https://docs.rs#375)//! // Emulates a type-level `InitState::Uninit` variant.
[376](https://docs.rs#376)//! // Marks a field as uninitialized.
[377](https://docs.rs#377)//! enum Uninit {}
[378](https://docs.rs#378)//!
[379](https://docs.rs#379)//! impl InitState for Uninit {
[380](https://docs.rs#380)//!     type BuilderField<T> = ();
[381](https://docs.rs#381)//! }
[382](https://docs.rs#382)//!
[383](https://docs.rs#383)//! typewit::simple_type_witness! {
[384](https://docs.rs#384)//!     // Declares `enum InitWit<__Wit>`, a type witness.
[385](https://docs.rs#385)//!     // (the `__Wit` type parameter is implicitly added after all generics)
[386](https://docs.rs#386)//!     enum InitWit {
[387](https://docs.rs#387)//!         // This variant requires `__Wit == Init`
[388](https://docs.rs#388)//!         InitW = Init,
[389](https://docs.rs#389)//!         // This variant requires `__Wit == Uninit`
[390](https://docs.rs#390)//!         UninitW = Uninit,
[391](https://docs.rs#391)//!     }
[392](https://docs.rs#392)//! }
[393](https://docs.rs#393)//! ```
[394](https://docs.rs#394)//!
[395](https://docs.rs#395)//! ### Generic Const Expressions
[396](https://docs.rs#396)//!
[397](https://docs.rs#397)//! This example uses [`Usize`] to coerce an arrays whose length is generic to
[398](https://docs.rs#398)//! another generic, but equal, length.
[399](https://docs.rs#399)//!
[400](https://docs.rs#400)//! This example requires the `"generic_const_exprs"` crate feature because it uses the
[401](https://docs.rs#401)//! currently-unstable [`generic_const_exprs`] language feature.
[402](https://docs.rs#402)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "generic_const_exprs"), doc = "```ignore")]
[403](https://docs.rs#403)#![cfg_attr(feature = "generic_const_exprs", doc = "```rust")]
[404](https://docs.rs#404)//! #![feature(generic_const_exprs)]
[405](https://docs.rs#405)//!
[406](https://docs.rs#406)//! use typewit::{const_marker::Usize, TypeCmp, TypeEq};
[407](https://docs.rs#407)//!
[408](https://docs.rs#408)//!
[409](https://docs.rs#409)//! let mut arrays = Arrays::<1, 3> { a: [3, 5, 8], b: [13, 21, 34] };
[410](https://docs.rs#410)//!
[411](https://docs.rs#411)//! arrays.swap_inner();
[412](https://docs.rs#412)//!
[413](https://docs.rs#413)//! assert_eq!(arrays.a, [13, 21, 34]);
[414](https://docs.rs#414)//! assert_eq!(arrays.b, [3, 5, 8]);
[415](https://docs.rs#415)//!
[416](https://docs.rs#416)//!
[417](https://docs.rs#417)//! struct Arrays<const A: usize, const B: usize>
[418](https://docs.rs#418)//! where
[419](https://docs.rs#419)//!     [u8; A * B]:,
[420](https://docs.rs#420)//!     [u8; B * A]:,
[421](https://docs.rs#421)//! {
[422](https://docs.rs#422)//!     a: [u8; A * B],
[423](https://docs.rs#423)//!     b: [u8; B * A],
[424](https://docs.rs#424)//! }
[425](https://docs.rs#425)//!
[426](https://docs.rs#426)//! impl<const A: usize, const B: usize> Arrays<A, B>
[427](https://docs.rs#427)//! where
[428](https://docs.rs#428)//!     [u8; A * B]:,
[429](https://docs.rs#429)//!     [u8; B * A]:,
[430](https://docs.rs#430)//! {
[431](https://docs.rs#431)//!     // Swaps the two array fields
[432](https://docs.rs#432)//!     const fn swap_inner(&mut self) {
[433](https://docs.rs#433)//!         let a = TypeEq::new::<u8>() // : TypeEq<u8, u8>
[434](https://docs.rs#434)//!             .in_array(commutative_proof::<A, B>()) // : TypeEq<[u8; A * B], [u8; B * A]>
[435](https://docs.rs#435)//!             .in_mut() // : TypeEq<&mut [u8; A * B], &mut [u8; B * A]>
[436](https://docs.rs#436)//!             .to_right(
[437](https://docs.rs#437)//!                 &mut self.a // : &mut [u8; A * B]
[438](https://docs.rs#438)//!             ); // : &mut [u8; B * A]
[439](https://docs.rs#439)//!
[440](https://docs.rs#440)//!         core::mem::swap(a, &mut self.b);
[441](https://docs.rs#441)//!     }
[442](https://docs.rs#442)//! }
[443](https://docs.rs#443)//!
[444](https://docs.rs#444)//! const fn commutative_proof<const A: usize, const B: usize>(
[445](https://docs.rs#445)//! ) -> TypeEq<Usize<{A * B}>, Usize<{B * A}>>
[446](https://docs.rs#446)//! {
[447](https://docs.rs#447)//!     // panic-safety: A * B == B * A always holds, so this `unwrap_eq` can never panic
[448](https://docs.rs#448)//!     Usize::<{A * B}>.equals(Usize::<{B * A}>).unwrap_eq()
[449](https://docs.rs#449)//! }
[450](https://docs.rs#450)//!
[451](https://docs.rs#451)//! ```
[452](https://docs.rs#452)//!
[453](https://docs.rs#453)//! If you tried to swap the fields directly, you'd get this error:
[454](https://docs.rs#454)//! ```text
[455](https://docs.rs#455)//! error[E0308]: mismatched types
[456](https://docs.rs#456)//!   --> src/lib.rs:437:38
[457](https://docs.rs#457)//!    |
[458](https://docs.rs#458)//! 42 |         core::mem::swap(&mut self.a, &mut self.b);
[459](https://docs.rs#459)//!    |                                      ^^^^^^^^^^^ expected `A * B`, found `B * A`
[460](https://docs.rs#460)//!    |
[461](https://docs.rs#461)//!    = note: expected constant `A * B`
[462](https://docs.rs#462)//!               found constant `B * A`
[463](https://docs.rs#463)//! ```
[464](https://docs.rs#464)//!
[465](https://docs.rs#465)//!
[466](https://docs.rs#466)//! # Cargo features
[467](https://docs.rs#467)//!
[468](https://docs.rs#468)//! These are the features of this crate.
[469](https://docs.rs#469)//!
[470](https://docs.rs#470)//! ### Default-features

# TypeEq in typewit - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/typewit/1.15.2/typewit/struct.TypeEq.html

## Expand description

Value-level proof that `L` is the same type as `R`

This type can be used to prove that `L` and `R` are the same type,
because it can only be safely constructed with
[ TypeEq::<L, L>::NEW](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.NEW)(or

[), where both type arguments are the same type.](https://docs.rs#method.new)

`new`This type is not too useful by itself, it becomes useful
[when put inside of an enum](https://docs.rs#polymorphic-branching).

`TypeEq<L, R>` uses the `L` type parameter as the more generic type by convention
(e.g: `TypeEq<T, char>`).
This only matters if you’re using the type witness traits
([ HasTypeWitness](https://docs.rs/trait.HasTypeWitness.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/trait.MakeTypeWitness.html)

`MakeTypeWitness`[) with](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeWitnessTypeArg.html)

`TypeWitnessTypeArg``TypeEq`.[§](https://docs.rs#soundness)Soundness

`TypeEq<L, R>` requires both type arguments to be the same type so that
[projecting](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeEq.html#method.project) the type arguments results in the same type for
both arguments.

Unsafely creating a `TypeEq<L, R>` where `L != R` allows
[transmuting between any two types](https://docs.rs#arbitrary-transmute)
(that is bad).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#polymorphic-branching)Polymorphic branching

This example demonstrates how type witnesses can be used to choose between expressions of different types with a constant.

```
use typewit::TypeEq;

const fn main() {
    assert!(matches!(choose!(0; b"a string", 2, panic!()), b"a string"));

    const UNO: u64 = 1;
    assert!(matches!(choose!(UNO; loop{}, [3, 5], true), [3, 5]));

    assert!(matches!(choose!(2 + 3; (), unreachable!(), ['5', '3']), ['5', '3']));
}

/// Evaluates the argument at position `$chosen % 3`, other arguments aren't evaluated.
///
/// The arguments can all be different types.
///
/// `$chosen` must be a `u64` constant.
#[macro_export]
macro_rules! choose {
    ($chosen:expr; $arg_0: expr, $arg_1: expr, $arg_2: expr) => {
        match Choice::<{$chosen % 3}>::VAL {
            // `te` (a `TypeEq<T, X>`) allows us to safely go between
            // the type that the match returns (its `T` type argument)
            // and the type of `$arg_0` (its `X` type argument).
            Branch3::A(te) => {
                // `to_left` goes from `X` to `T`
                te.to_left($arg_0)
            }
            // same as the `A` branch, with a different type for the argument
            Branch3::B(te) => te.to_left($arg_1),
            // same as the `A` branch, with a different type for the argument
            Branch3::C(te) => te.to_left($arg_2),
        }
    }
}

// This is a type witness
pub enum Branch3<T, X, Y, Z> {
    // This variant requires `T == X`
    A(TypeEq<T, X>),

    // This variant requires `T == Y`
    B(TypeEq<T, Y>),

    // This variant requires `T == Z`
    C(TypeEq<T, Z>),
}

// Used to get different values of `Branch3` depending on `N`
pub trait Choice<const N: u64> {
    const VAL: Self;
}

impl<X, Y, Z> Choice<0> for Branch3<X, X, Y, Z> {
    // Because the first two type arguments of `Branch3` are `X`
    // (as required by the `TypeEq<T, X>` field in Branch3's type definition),
    // we can use `TypeEq::NEW` here.
    const VAL: Self = Self::A(TypeEq::NEW);
}

impl<X, Y, Z> Choice<1> for Branch3<Y, X, Y, Z> {
    const VAL: Self = Self::B(TypeEq::NEW);
}

impl<X, Y, Z> Choice<2> for Branch3<Z, X, Y, Z> {
    const VAL: Self = Self::C(TypeEq::NEW);
}

```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Constructs a `TypeEq<T, T>`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use typewit::TypeEq;

assert_eq!(mutate(5, Wit::U32(TypeEq::NEW)), 25);

assert_eq!(mutate(5, Wit::Other(TypeEq::NEW)), 5);
assert_eq!(mutate("hello", Wit::Other(TypeEq::NEW)), "hello");

const fn mutate<W>(val: W, wit: Wit<W>) -> W {
    match wit {
        Wit::U32(te) => te.to_left(te.to_right(val) + 20),
        Wit::Other(_) => val,
    }
}

// This can't be written using the `simple_type_witness` macro because the
// type in the `Other` variant overlaps with the other ones.
enum Wit<W> {
    U32(TypeEq<W, u32>),
    Other(TypeEq<W, W>),
}
```
Constructs `TypeEq<L, R>` if `L == R`, otherwise returns None.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use typewit::TypeEq;

use std::any::Any;

assert_eq!(sum_u32s(&[3u32, 5, 8]), Some(16));
assert_eq!(sum_u32s(&[3i32, 5, 8]), None);

fn sum_u32s<T: Clone + Any>(foo: &[T]) -> Option<u32> {
    typecast_slice::<T, u32>(foo)
        .map(|foo: &[u32]| foo.iter().copied().sum())
}

fn typecast_slice<T: Any, U: Any>(foo: &[T]) -> Option<&[U]> {
    struct SliceFn;
    impl<T> typewit::TypeFn<T> for SliceFn {
        type Output = [T];
    }

    TypeEq::<T, U>::with_any().map(|te: TypeEq<T, U>|{
        te.map(SliceFn) // TypeEq<[T], [U]>
          .in_ref()   // TypeEq<&[T]>, &[U]>
          .to_right(foo) // identity cast from `&[T]` to `&[U]`
    })
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/typewit/type_eq.rs.html#426-428)#### pub const unsafe fn [new_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.new_unchecked)() -> [TypeEq](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeEq.html)<L, R>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/typewit/type_eq.rs.html#426-428)

#### pub const unsafe fn [new_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.new_unchecked)() -> [TypeEq](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeEq.html)<L, R>

Constructs a `TypeEq<L, R>`.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

You must ensure that `L` is the same type as `R`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-1)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#unsound-usage)Unsound usage

This example demonstrates why `L == R` is a strict requirement.

```
use typewit::{TypeEq, TypeFn};
// SAFETY: WRONG! UNSOUND!
let te: TypeEq<u8, i8> = unsafe{ TypeEq::new_unchecked() };

// Because `TypeEq<u8, i8>` is incorrect,
// we get this absurd `TypeEq` from the `project` method.
let absurd: TypeEq<(), Vec<usize>> = te.project::<Func>();

// This casts from `()` to `Vec<usize>` (which is UB).
// Last time I tried uncommenting this, it killed the test runner.
// absurd.to_right(());

struct Func;
impl TypeFn<u8> for Func { type Output = (); }
impl TypeFn<i8> for Func { type Output = Vec<usize>; }
```
Swaps the type parameters of this `TypeEq`

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
use typewit::TypeEq;

assert_eq!(flip_bytes([3, 5], TypeEq::NEW), [5, 3]);

const fn flip_bytes<T>(val: T, te: TypeEq<T, [u8; 2]>) -> T {
    bar(val, te.flip())
}
const fn bar<T>(val: T, te: TypeEq<[u8; 2], T>) -> T {
    let [l, r] = te.to_left(val);
    te.to_right([r, l])
}
```
Joins this `TypeEq<L, R>` with a `TypeEq<R, O>`, producing a `TypeEq<L, O>`.

The returned `TypeEq` can then be used to coerce between `L` and `O`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-4)Example

```
use typewit::TypeEq;

assert_eq!(foo(TypeEq::NEW, TypeEq::NEW, Some(3)), Some(3));
assert_eq!(foo(TypeEq::NEW, TypeEq::NEW, None), None);

fn foo<L, X>(
    this: TypeEq<L, Option<X>>,
    that: TypeEq<Option<X>, Option<u32>>,
    value: Option<u32>,
) -> L {
    let te: TypeEq<L, Option<u32>> = this.join(that);
    te.to_left(value)
}

```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/typewit/type_eq.rs.html#559-564)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/typewit/type_eq.rs.html#559-564)

Combines this `TypeEq<L0, R0>` with a `TypeEq<L1, R1>`,
producing a `TypeEq<(L0, L1), (R0, R1)>`.

[§](https://docs.rs#alternative)Alternative

For an alternative which allows zipping `TypeEq` with any
[ BaseTypeWitness](https://docs.rs/trait.BaseTypeWitness.html),
you can use

[(requires the](https://docs.rs/methods/fn.zip2.html)

`methods::zip2``"rust_1_65"` feature)[§](https://docs.rs#example-5)Example

This example demonstrates how one can combine two `TypeEq`s to use
with a multi-parameter type.

```
use typewit::{const_marker::Usize, TypeEq, TypeFn};

assert_eq!(make_foo(TypeEq::NEW, TypeEq::NEW), Foo("hello", [3, 5, 8]));

const fn make_foo<T, const N: usize>(
    te_ty: TypeEq<T, &'static str>,
    te_len: TypeEq<Usize<N>, Usize<3>>,
) -> Foo<T, N> {
    // the type annotations are just for the reader, they can be inferred.
    let te_pair: TypeEq<(T, Usize<N>), (&str, Usize<3>)> = te_ty.zip(te_len);

    let te: TypeEq<Foo<T, N>, Foo<&str, 3>> = te_pair.project::<GFoo>();

    // `te.to_left(...)` here goes from `Foo<&str, 3>` to `Foo<T, N>`
    te.to_left(Foo("hello", [3, 5, 8]))
}

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Foo<T, const N: usize>(T, [u8; N]);

typewit::type_fn!{
    // Type-level function from `(T, Usize<N>)` to `Foo<T, N>`
    struct GFoo;
    impl<T, const N: usize> (T, Usize<N>) => Foo<T, N>
}
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/typewit/type_eq.rs.html#595-605)#### pub const fn [zip3](https://docs.rs#method.zip3)<L1, R1, L2: ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html), R2: ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)>(
    self: [TypeEq](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeEq.html)<L0, R0>,

Combines three `TypeEq<L*, R*>` to produce a
`TypeEq<(L0, L1, L2), (R0, R1, R2)>`.

[§](https://docs.rs#alternative-1)Alternative

For an alternative which allows zipping `TypeEq` with two of any
[ BaseTypeWitness](https://docs.rs/trait.BaseTypeWitness.html),
you can use

[(requires the](https://docs.rs/methods/fn.zip3.html)

`methods::zip3``"rust_1_65"` feature)[§](https://docs.rs#example-6)Example

```
use typewit::{TypeEq, type_eq};

use std::cmp::Ordering::{self, Less};

assert_eq!(make_tuple(type_eq(), type_eq(), type_eq()), (3, "foo", Less));

fn make_tuple<A, B, C>(
    te0: TypeEq<A, u8>,
    te1: TypeEq<B, &str>,
    te2: TypeEq<C, Ordering>,
) -> (A, B, C) {
    te0.zip3(te1, te2) // returns `TypeEq<(A, B, C), (u8, &str, Ordering)>`
        .to_left((3, "foo", Less))
}

Combines four `TypeEq<L*, R*>` to produce a
`TypeEq<(L0, L1, L2, L3), (R0, R1, R2, L3)>`.

[§](https://docs.rs#alternative-2)Alternative

For an alternative which allows zipping `TypeEq` with three of any
[ BaseTypeWitness](https://docs.rs/trait.BaseTypeWitness.html),
you can use

[(requires the](https://docs.rs/methods/fn.zip4.html)

`methods::zip4``"rust_1_65"` feature)[§](https://docs.rs#example-7)Example

```
use typewit::{TypeEq, type_eq};

use std::cmp::Ordering::{self, Less};

assert_eq!(
    make_tuple(type_eq(), type_eq(), type_eq(), type_eq()),
    (3, "foo", Less, true),
);

fn make_tuple<A, B, C, D>(
    te0: TypeEq<A, u8>,
    te1: TypeEq<B, &str>,
    te2: TypeEq<C, Ordering>,
    te3: TypeEq<D, bool>,
) -> (A, B, C, D) {
    let te: TypeEq<(A, B, C, D), (u8, &str, Ordering, bool)> = te0.zip4(te1, te2, te3);
    te.to_left((3, "foo", Less, true))
}

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/typewit/type_eq.rs.html#687-694)#### pub const fn [reachability_hint](https://docs.rs#method.reachability_hint)<T>(self, val: T) -> T

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/typewit/type_eq.rs.html#687-694)

#### pub const fn [reachability_hint](https://docs.rs#method.reachability_hint)<T>(self, val: T) -> T

Hints to the compiler that a `TypeEq<L, R>`
can only be constructed if `L == R`.

This function takes and returns `val` unmodified.
This allows returning some value from an expression
while hinting that `L == R`.

A no-op cast from `L` to `R`.

This cast is a no-op because having a `TypeEq<L, R>` value
proves that `L` and `R` are the same type.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-8)Example

```
use typewit::{TypeEq, type_eq};

use std::cmp::Ordering::{self, *};

assert_eq!(mutated(Less, Wit::Ord(type_eq())), Greater);
assert_eq!(mutated(Equal, Wit::Ord(type_eq())), Equal);
assert_eq!(mutated(Greater, Wit::Ord(type_eq())), Less);

assert_eq!(mutated(false, Wit::Bool(type_eq())), true);
assert_eq!(mutated(true, Wit::Bool(type_eq())), false);

const fn mutated<R>(arg: R, w: Wit<R>) -> R {
    match w {
        Wit::Ord(te) => te.to_left(te.to_right(arg).reverse()),
        Wit::Bool(te) => te.to_left(!te.to_right(arg)),
    }
}

enum Wit<R> {
    Ord(TypeEq<R, Ordering>),
    Bool(TypeEq<R, bool>),
}
```
A no-op cast from `R` to `L`.

This cast is a no-op because having a `TypeEq<L, R>` value
proves that `L` and `R` are the same type.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-9)Example

```
use typewit::{TypeEq, type_eq};

assert_eq!(stuff(Wit::OptSlice(type_eq())), Some(&[3, 5, 8][..]));
assert_eq!(stuff(Wit::Bool(type_eq())), true);

const fn stuff<R>(te: Wit<R>) -> R {
    match te {
        Wit::OptSlice(te) => te.to_left(Some(&[3, 5, 8])),
        Wit::Bool(te) => te.to_left(true),
    }
}

enum Wit<R> {
    OptSlice(TypeEq<R, Option<&'static [u16]>>),
    Bool(TypeEq<R, bool>),
}
```
Maps the type arguments of this `TypeEq`
by using the `F` [type-level function](https://docs.rs/type_fn/trait.TypeFn.html).

Use this function over [ project](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeEq.html#method.project)
if you want the type of the passed in function to be inferred.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-10)Example

```
use typewit::{TypeEq, TypeFn};

assert_eq!(foo(TypeEq::NEW), (false, 5));

const fn foo<'a, T>(te: TypeEq<u32, T>) -> (bool, T) {
    // `GPair<bool>` maps `u32` to `(bool, u32)`
    //           and maps `T`   to `(bool, T)`
    let map_te: TypeEq<(bool, u32), (bool, T)> = te.map(GPair::<bool>::NEW);

    // same as the above, but inferring `GPair`'s generic arguments.
    let _: TypeEq<(bool, u32), (bool, T)> = te.map(GPair::NEW);

    map_te.to_right((false, 5u32))
}

// Declares `struct GPair<A>`, a type-level function from `B` to `(A, B)`
typewit::type_fn! {
     struct GPair<A>;

     impl<B> B => (A, B)
}
```
Maps the type arguments of this `TypeEq`
by using the `F` [type-level function](https://docs.rs/type_fn/trait.TypeFn.html).

Use this function over [ map](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeEq.html#method.map)
if you want to specify the type of the passed in function explicitly.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-11)Example

```
use typewit::{TypeEq, TypeFn};

assert_eq!(foo(TypeEq::NEW), vec![3u32, 5, 8]);

fn foo<T>(te: TypeEq<u32, T>) -> Vec<T> {

    vec_te.to_right(vec![3, 5, 8])
}

// Declares `GVec`, a type-level function from `T` to `Vec<T>`

Use this function over [ unproject](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeEq.html#method.unproject)

[§](https://docs.rs#example-12)Example

```
use typewit::{TypeEq, UncallFn};

assert_eq!(first_int(&[3, 5, 8, 13], TypeEq::NEW), 3);

const fn first_int<T, const N: usize>(
    array: &[T; N],
    te_slice: TypeEq<[T], [u8]>,
) -> u8 {
    let te: TypeEq<T, u8> = te_slice.unmap(SliceFn);
    let te_ref: TypeEq<&T, &u8> = te.in_ref();
    *te_ref.to_right(&array[0])
}

    struct SliceFn;

    impl<T> T => [T]
}

Maps the type arguments of this `TypeEq`
by using the [reversed](https://docs.rs/type_fn/trait.RevTypeFn.html)
version of the `F` type-level function.

Use this function over [ unmap](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeEq.html#method.unmap)
if you want to specify the type of the passed in function explicitly.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-13)Example

```
use typewit::TypeEq;
use std::ops::{Range, RangeInclusive as RangeInc};

assert_eq!(usize_bounds(3..=5, TypeEq::NEW), (3, 5));

const fn usize_bounds<T>(
    range: RangeInc<T>,
    te_range: TypeEq<Range<T>, Range<usize>>,
) -> (usize, usize) {
    let te: TypeEq<T, usize> = te_range.unproject::<RangeFn>();

    let te_range_inc: TypeEq<RangeInc<T>, RangeInc<usize>> = te.project::<RangeIncFn>();

    let range: RangeInc<usize> = te_range_inc.to_right(range);

    (*range.start(), *range.end())
}

typewit::inj_type_fn! {
    struct RangeFn;

    impl<T> T => Range<T>
}
typewit::inj_type_fn! {
    struct RangeIncFn;

    impl<T> T => RangeInc<T>
}

Converts a `TypeEq<L, R>` to `TypeEq<&L, &R>`

[§](https://docs.rs#example-14)Example

```
use typewit::{MakeTypeWitness, TypeEq};

assert_eq!(get::<u8>(), &3);
assert_eq!(get::<str>(), "hello");

const fn get<R: ?Sized>() -> &'static R
where
    Returned<R>: MakeTypeWitness
{
    match MakeTypeWitness::MAKE {
        // `te` is a `TypeEq<R, u8>`
        Returned::U8(te) => te.in_ref().to_left(&3),
        // `te` is a `TypeEq<R, str>`
        Returned::Str(te) => te.in_ref().to_left("hello"),
    }
}

typewit::simple_type_witness! {
    // declares the `enum Returned<R> {` type witness
    enum Returned {
        // this variant requires `R == u8`
        U8 = u8,
        // this variant requires `R == str`
        Str = str,
    }
}
```

`rust_1_83`Converts a `TypeEq<L, R>` to `TypeEq<&mut L, &mut R>`

[§](https://docs.rs#constness)Constness

This requires the `"rust_1_83"` feature to be a `const fn`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-15)Example

Because this example calls `in_mut` inside a `const fn`,
it requires the `"rust_1_83"` crate feature.

```

 use typewit::{TypeEq, type_eq};

 let foo = &mut Foo { bar: 10, baz: ['W', 'H', 'O'] };

 *get_mut(foo, Field::Bar(type_eq())) *= 2;
 assert_eq!(foo.bar, 20);

 assert_eq!(*get_mut(foo, Field::Baz(type_eq())), ['W', 'H', 'O']);

 const fn get_mut<R>(foo: &mut Foo, te: Field<R>) -> &mut R {
     match te {
         Field::Bar(te) => te.in_mut().to_left(&mut foo.bar),
         Field::Baz(te) => te.in_mut().to_left(&mut foo.baz),
     }
 }

 struct Foo {
     bar: u8,
     baz: [char; 3],
 }

 enum Field<R: ?Sized> {
     Bar(TypeEq<R, u8>),
     Baz(TypeEq<R, [char; 3]>),
 }

Converts a `TypeEq<L, R>` to `TypeEq<Box<L>, Box<R>>`

[§](https://docs.rs#example-16)Example

```
use typewit::{MakeTypeWitness, TypeEq, type_eq};

use std::any::Any;
use std::fmt::Display;

assert_eq!(factory::<dyn Any>().downcast::<u16>().unwrap(), Box::new(1337));
assert_eq!(factory::<dyn Display>().to_string(), "hello bob");

fn factory<R: ?Sized>() -> Box<R>
where
    Dyn<R>: MakeTypeWitness
{
    match MakeTypeWitness::MAKE {
        // `te` is a `TypeEq<R, dyn Any>`
        Dyn::Any(te) => te.in_box().to_left(Box::new(1337u16)),
        // `te` is a `TypeEq<R, dyn Display>`
        Dyn::Display(te) => te.in_box().to_left(Box::new("hello bob")),
    }
}

typewit::simple_type_witness! {
    // declares the `enum Dyn<R> {` type witness
    enum Dyn {
        // this variant requires `R == dyn Any`
        Any = dyn Any,
        // this variant requires `R == dyn Display`
        Display = dyn Display,
    }
}

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/typewit/type_eq.rs.html#1171-1182)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/typewit/type_eq.rs.html#1171-1182)

Combines `TypeEq<L, R>` and `TypeEq<Usize<UL>, Usize<UR>>`
into `TypeEq<[L; UL], [R; UR]>`

[§](https://docs.rs#alternative-3)Alternative

For an alternative which allows passing any
[ BaseTypeWitness](https://docs.rs/trait.BaseTypeWitness.html) for the length,
you can use

[(requires the](https://docs.rs/methods/fn.in_array.html)

`methods::in_array``"rust_1_65"` feature)[§](https://docs.rs#example-17)Example

**motivation**

The safe way to map an array in const fns(on stable Rust in 2023) is to create an array of the returned type with some dummy value, and then fill it in with the desired values.

Because the function in this example takes a `[T; LEN]` where the `T` is generic,
it copies the first element of the input array to initialize the returned array,
so we must handle empty arrays,
but trying to return an empty array the naive way

does not work

```
error[E0308]: mismatched types
 --> src/type_eq.rs:827:16
  |
4 | const fn map_wrapping<T: Copy, const LEN: usize>(arr: [T; LEN]) -> [Wrapping<T>; LEN] {
  |                                                                    ------------------ expected `[Wrapping<T>; LEN]` because of return type
5 |     if LEN == 0 {
6 |         return [];
  |                ^^ expected `LEN`, found `0`
  |
  = note: expected array `[Wrapping<T>; LEN]`
             found array `[_; 0]`

```
This example demonstrates how `in_array` allows one to return an empty array:
(this example requires Rust 1.61.0, because it uses trait bounds in const fns)

```
use typewit::{const_marker::Usize, TypeCmp, TypeEq};

use std::num::Wrapping;

assert_eq!(map_wrapping([""; 0]), []);
assert_eq!(map_wrapping([3, 5, 8]), [Wrapping(3), Wrapping(5), Wrapping(8)]);

const fn map_wrapping<T: Copy, const LEN: usize>(arr: [T; LEN]) -> [Wrapping<T>; LEN] {
    // `teq` is a `TypeEq<Usize<LEN>, Usize<0>>`
    if let TypeCmp::Eq(teq) = Usize::<LEN>.equals(Usize::<0>) {
        return TypeEq::new::<Wrapping<T>>()
            .in_array(teq) // `TypeEq<[Wrapping<T>; LEN], [Wrapping<T>; 0]>`
            .to_left([]);
    }

    let mut ret = [Wrapping(arr[0]); LEN];
    let mut i = 1;

    while i < LEN {
        ret[i] = Wrapping(arr[i]);
        i += 1;
    }

    ret
}
```

# TypeFn in typewit::type_fn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/typewit/1.15.2/typewit/type_fn/trait.TypeFn.html

`pub trait TypeFn<T: ?`[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)> {
    type [Output](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Output): ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html);
    const [TYPE_FN_ASSERTS](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.TYPE_FN_ASSERTS): [()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.unit.html) = ();
}## Expand description

A function that operates purely on the level of types.

These can be used in `typewit` to
[map the type arguments of  TypeEq](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeEq.html#method.project).

Type-level functions can also be declared with the
[ type_fn](https://docs.rs/macro.type_fn.html) macro.

[§](https://docs.rs#properties)Properties

These are properties about `TypeFn` implementors that users can rely on.

For any given `F: TypeFn<A> + TypeFn<B>` these hold:

- If `A == B`, then`CallFn<F, A> == CallFn<F, B>`.
- If `CallFn<F, A> != CallFn<F, B>`, then`A != B`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#manual-implementation)Manual Implementation

```
use typewit::{TypeFn, CallFn};

let string: CallFn<AddOutput<String>, &str> = "foo".to_string() +  ", bar";
let _: String = string;
assert_eq!(string, "foo, bar");

struct AddOutput<Lhs>(core::marker::PhantomData<Lhs>);

// This part is optional,
// only necessary to pass the function as a value, not just as a type.
impl<Lhs> AddOutput<Lhs> {
    const NEW: Self = Self(core::marker::PhantomData);
}

impl<Lhs, Rhs> TypeFn<Rhs> for AddOutput<Lhs>
where
    Lhs: core::ops::Add<Rhs>
{
    type Output = Lhs::Output;
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#macro-based-implementation)Macro-based Implementation

This example uses the [ type_fn](https://docs.rs/macro.type_fn.html) macro
to declare the type-level function,
and is otherwise equivalent to the manual one.

```
use typewit::CallFn;

let string: CallFn<AddOutput<String>, &str> = "foo".to_string() +  ", bar";
let _: String = string;
assert_eq!(string, "foo, bar");

typewit::type_fn! {
    struct AddOutput<Lhs>;

    impl<Rhs> Rhs => Lhs::Output
    where Lhs: core::ops::Add<Rhs>
}
```

# Usize in typewit::const_marker - Rust

`pub struct Usize<const VAL: `[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.usize.html)>;## Expand description

Marker type for passing `const VAL: usize` as a type parameter.

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-compatibility)Serde compatibility

When the `"serde"` feature is enabled,
this type is serialized/deserialized as the `VAL` const parameter.

```
use typewit::const_marker::Usize;

assert_eq!(serde_json::from_str::<Usize<1>>("1").unwrap(), Usize::<1>);

// trying to deserialize `Usize<1>` from any value other than `1` produces an error
assert!(serde_json::from_str::<Usize<1>>("0").is_err());

assert_eq!(serde_json::to_string(&Usize::<1>).unwrap(), "1");

assert_eq!(serde_json::to_string(&Usize::<92>).unwrap(), "92");

```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/typewit/const_marker.rs.html#300-394)superceeded by `equals` method

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/typewit/const_marker.rs.html#300-394)

superceeded by `equals` method

Compares `self` and `other` for equality.

Returns:

- `Ok(TypeEq)`: if- `VAL == OTHER`
- `Err(TypeNe)`: if- `VAL != OTHER`

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/typewit/const_marker.rs.html#300-394)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/typewit/const_marker.rs.html#300-394)

Compares `self` and `other` for equality.

Returns:

- `TypeCmp::Eq(TypeEq)`: if- `VAL == OTHER`
- `TypeCmp::Ne(TypeNe)`: if- `VAL != OTHER`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#array)Array

This example demonstrates how `Usize` can be used to
specialize behavior on array length.

(this example requires Rust 1.61.0, because it uses trait bounds in const fns)

```
 use typewit::{const_marker::Usize, TypeCmp, TypeEq};

 assert_eq!(try_from_pair::<_, 0>((3, 5)), Ok([]));
 assert_eq!(try_from_pair::<_, 1>((3, 5)), Ok([3]));
 assert_eq!(try_from_pair::<_, 2>((3, 5)), Ok([3, 5]));
 assert_eq!(try_from_pair::<_, 3>((3, 5)), Err((3, 5)));

 const fn try_from_pair<T: Copy, const LEN: usize>(pair: (T, T)) -> Result<[T; LEN], (T, T)> {
     if let TypeCmp::Eq(te_len) = Usize::<LEN>.equals(Usize::<0>) {
         // this branch is ran on `LEN == 0`
         // `te_len` is a `TypeEq<Usize<LEN>, Usize<0>>`
         Ok(
             TypeEq::new::<T>()    // `TypeEq<T, T>`
                 .in_array(te_len) // `TypeEq<[T; LEN], [T; 0]>`
                 .to_left([])      // Goes from `[T; 0]` to `[T; LEN]`
         )
     } else if let TypeCmp::Eq(te_len) = Usize.equals(Usize) {
         // this branch is ran on `LEN == 1`
         // `te_len` is inferred to be `TypeEq<Usize<LEN>, Usize<1>>`
         Ok(TypeEq::NEW.in_array(te_len).to_left([pair.0]))
     } else if let TypeCmp::Eq(te_len) = Usize.equals(Usize) {
         // this branch is ran on `LEN == 2`
         // `te_len` is inferred to be `TypeEq<Usize<LEN>, Usize<2>>`
         Ok(TypeEq::NEW.in_array(te_len).to_left([pair.0, pair.1]))
     } else {
         Err(pair)
     }
 }

```
[§](https://docs.rs#struct)Struct

This example demonstrates how `Usize` can be used to pass a
const-generic struct to a function expecting a concrete type of that struct.

```
use typewit::{const_marker::Usize, TypeCmp};
assert_eq!(mutate(Array([])), Array([]));
assert_eq!(mutate(Array([3])), Array([3]));
assert_eq!(mutate(Array([3, 5])), Array([3, 5]));
assert_eq!(mutate(Array([3, 5, 8])), Array([8, 5, 3])); // reversed!
assert_eq!(mutate(Array([3, 5, 8, 13])), Array([3, 5, 8, 13]));
#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
struct Array<const CAP: usize>([u32; CAP]);
const fn mutate<const LEN: usize>(arr: Array<LEN>) -> Array<LEN> {
    match Usize::<LEN>.equals(Usize::<3>) {
        // `te_len` is a `TypeEq<Usize<LEN>, Usize<3>>`
        // this branch is ran on `LEN == 3`
        TypeCmp::Eq(te_len) => {
            // `te` is a `TypeEq<Array<LEN>, Array<3>>`
            let te = te_len.project::<GArray>();
            // `te.to_right(...)` here goes from `Array<LEN>` to `Array<3>`
            let ret = reverse3(te.to_right(arr));
            // `te.to_left(...)` here goes from `Array<3>` to `Array<LEN>`
            te.to_left(ret)
        }
        TypeCmp::Ne(_) => arr,
    }
}
const fn reverse3(Array([a, b, c]): Array<3>) -> Array<3> {
    Array([c, b, a])
}
typewit::type_fn!{
    // Type-level function from `Usize<LEN>` to `Array<LEN>`
    struct GArray;
    impl<const LEN: usize> Usize<LEN> => Array<LEN>
}
```

# typewit::const_marker - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/typewit/1.15.2/typewit/const_marker/index.html

## Expand description

Marker types for passing constants as type arguments.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

This example emulates specialization,
eliding a `.clone()` call when the created array is only one element long.

```
use typewit::{const_marker::Usize, TypeCmp, TypeEq};

let arr = [3u8, 5, 8];

assert_eq!(repeat(3), []);
assert_eq!(repeat(3), [3]);
assert_eq!(repeat(3), [3, 3]);
assert_eq!(repeat(3), [3, 3, 3]);
assert_eq!(repeat(3), [3, 3, 3, 3]);

fn repeat<T: Clone, const OUT: usize>(val: T) -> [T; OUT] {
    // `te_len` ìs a `TypeEq<Usize<OUT>, Usize<1>>`
    if let TypeCmp::Eq(te_len) = Usize::<OUT>.equals(Usize::<1>) {
        // This branch is ran when `OUT == 1`
        TypeEq::new::<T>()    // returns `TypeEq<T, T>`
            .in_array(te_len) // returns `TypeEq<[T; OUT], [T; 1]>`
            .to_left([val])   // goes from `[T; 1]` to `[T; OUT]`
    } else {
        // This branch is ran when `OUT != 1`
        [(); OUT].map(|_| val.clone())
    }
}
```

# ConstMarker in typewit::const_marker - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/typewit/1.15.2/typewit/const_marker/trait.ConstMarker.html

## Expand description

A type that represents a constant

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

Emulating generic associated constants on stable

(this example Requires Rust 1.65.0)

```
use typewit::const_marker::{ConstMarker, ConstMarkerOf};

assert_eq!(make_array::<u8>(), ([3], [3, 3, 3]));

assert_eq!(make_array::<&str>(), (["hi"], ["hi", "hi", "hi"]));

const fn make_array<T: MakeArray>() -> ([T; 1], [T; 3]) {
    (T::Make::<1>::VAL, T::Make::<3>::VAL)
}

// `MakeArray` can make arrays of any length without writing a bound for each length!!
trait MakeArray: Sized {
    // emulates `const Make<const N: usize>: [Self; N];` (a generic associated constant)
    type Make<const N: usize>: ConstMarkerOf<[Self; N]>;
}

impl MakeArray for u8 {
    type Make<const N: usize> = MakeArrayConst<Self, N>;
}
impl<'a> MakeArray for &'a str {
    type Make<const N: usize> = MakeArrayConst<Self, N>;
}

struct MakeArrayConst<T, const N: usize>(core::marker::PhantomData<T>);

impl<const N: usize> ConstMarker for MakeArrayConst<u8, N> {
    type Of = [u8; N];
    const VAL: Self::Of = [3; N];
}

impl<'a, const N: usize> ConstMarker for MakeArrayConst<&'a str, N> {
    type Of = [&'a str; N];
    const VAL: Self::Of = ["hi"; N];
}

```

Calls the `F` [type-level function](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeFn.html) with `T` as its argument.

For `F:`[ InjTypeFn<T>](https://docs.rs/trait.InjTypeFn.html), it’s better to

```
use typewit::CallFn;

    L: core::ops::Mul<R>

    l * r
}

# CallInjFn in typewit::type_fn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/typewit/1.15.2/typewit/type_fn/type.CallInjFn.html

## Expand description

[ CallFn](https://docs.rs/type.CallFn.html) with an additional

`F:`[requirement, which helps with type inference.](https://docs.rs/trait.InjTypeFn.html)

`InjTypeFn<A>`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use typewit::{InjTypeFn, CallInjFn};

// inferred return type
let inferred_ret = upcast(3u8);
assert_eq!(inferred_ret, 3);

// inferred argument type
let inferred_arg: u32 = upcast(5);
assert_eq!(inferred_arg, 5);

// Because the return type is `CallInjFn<_, I>`,
// this can infer `I` from the return type,
fn upcast<I>(int: I) -> CallInjFn<Upcast, I>
where
    Upcast: InjTypeFn<I>,
    CallInjFn<Upcast, I>: From<I>,
{
    int.into()
}

typewit::inj_type_fn!{
    struct Upcast;

    impl u8 => u16;
    impl u16 => u32;
    impl u32 => u64;
    impl u64 => u128;
}
```
As of October 2023, replacing `CallInjFn` with `CallFn` can cause type inference errors:

```

  --> src/type_fn/injective.rs:132:32
   |
11 | let inferred_arg: u32 = upcast(5);
   |                         ------ ^ the trait `TypeFn<{integer}>` is not implemented for `Upcast`
   |                         |
   |                         required by a bound introduced by this call
   |
   = help: the following other types implement trait `TypeFn<T>`:
             <Upcast as TypeFn<u16>>
             <Upcast as TypeFn<u32>>
             <Upcast as TypeFn<u64>>
             <Upcast as TypeFn<u8>>
```

# InjTypeFn in typewit::type_fn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/typewit/1.15.2/typewit/type_fn/trait.InjTypeFn.html

`pub trait InjTypeFn<A: ?`[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)>: [TypeFn](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeFn.html)<A, Output = Self::[Ret](https://docs.rs/trait.InjTypeFn.html#associatedtype.Ret)> + [RevTypeFn](https://docs.rs/trait.RevTypeFn.html)<Self::[Ret](https://docs.rs/trait.InjTypeFn.html#associatedtype.Ret), Arg = A> {
    type [Ret](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Ret): ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html);
}## Expand description

An  [injective](https://docs.rs/index.html#injective)  type-level function

This trait is implemented automatically when both
[ TypeFn](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeFn.html) and

[are implemented, and the function is](https://docs.rs/trait.RevTypeFn.html)

`RevTypeFn`[injective](https://docs.rs/index.html#injective).

`InjTypeFn` cannot be manually implemented.[§](https://docs.rs#properties)Properties

These are properties about `InjTypeFn` that users can rely on.

For any given `F: InjTypeFn<A> + InjTypeFn<B>` these hold:

- If `A == B`, then`CallInjFn<F, A> == CallInjFn<F, B>`.
- If `CallInjFn<F, A> == CallInjFn<F, B>`, then`A == B`.
- If `A != B`, then`CallInjFn<F, A> != CallInjFn<F, B>`.
- If `CallInjFn<F, A> != CallInjFn<F, B>`, then`A != B`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#macro-based-implementation)Macro-based Implementation

```
use typewit::{CallInjFn, UncallFn, inj_type_fn};

let _: CallInjFn<BoxFn, u32> = Box::new(3u32);
let _: UncallFn<BoxFn, Box<u32>> = 3u32;

inj_type_fn!{
    struct BoxFn;

    impl<T: ?Sized> T => Box<T>
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-macro-implementation)Non-macro Implementation

```
use typewit::{CallInjFn, RevTypeFn, TypeFn, UncallFn};

let _: CallInjFn<BoxFn, u32> = Box::new(3u32);
let _: UncallFn<BoxFn, Box<u32>> = 3u32;

struct BoxFn;
impl<T: ?Sized> TypeFn<T> for BoxFn {
    type Output = Box<T>;

    // Asserts that this impl of `TypeFn` for `BoxFn` is injective.
    const TYPE_FN_ASSERTS: () = { let _: CallInjFn<Self, T>; };
}

impl<T: ?Sized> RevTypeFn<Box<T>> for BoxFn {
    type Arg = T;
}

```

# RevTypeFn in typewit::type_fn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/typewit/1.15.2/typewit/type_fn/trait.RevTypeFn.html

## Expand description

The inverse of [ TypeFn](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeFn.html),
for getting the argument of a

[from its return value.](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeFn.html)

`TypeFn`[§](https://docs.rs#properties)Properties

These are properties about `RevTypeFn` that users can rely on.

For any given `F: RevTypeFn<R> + RevTypeFn<O>` these hold:

-
If `R == O`, then`UncallFn<F, R> == UncallFn<F, O>`
-
If `R != O`, then`UncallFn<F, R> != UncallFn<F, O>`

Disclaimer: this trait **does not** by itself ensure that a function is
[injective](https://docs.rs/index.html#injective),
since `RevTypeFn<Ret>` can’t know if `Self::Arg` is the only argument
that could produce `Ret`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#macro-based-impl)Macro-based impl

```
use std::ops::Range;
use typewit::{RevTypeFn, UncallFn};
let array = [3usize, 5];
// Getting the argument of `ArrayFn` from its return value
let value: UncallFn<ArrayFn<2>, [usize; 2]> = array[0];
assert_eq!(value, 3usize);
typewit::inj_type_fn!{
    struct ArrayFn<const N: usize>;
    impl<T> T => [T; N]
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#manual-impl)Manual impl

```
use std::ops::Range;
use typewit::{CallInjFn, RevTypeFn, TypeFn, UncallFn};
let array = [3usize, 5];
// Getting the argument of `ArrayFn` from its return value
let value: UncallFn<ArrayFn<2>, [usize; 2]> = array[0];
assert_eq!(value, 3usize);
struct ArrayFn<const N: usize>;
impl<T, const N: usize> TypeFn<T> for ArrayFn<N> {
    type Output = [T; N];
    // Ensures that this impl of `TypeFn` for `ArrayFn` is injective.
    const TYPE_FN_ASSERTS: () = { let _: CallInjFn<Self, T>; };
}
impl<T, const N: usize> RevTypeFn<[T; N]> for ArrayFn<N> {
    type Arg = T;
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-injective-function)Non-injective function

As mentioned above, this trait doesn’t make a function [injective](https://docs.rs/index.html#injective).

In the example below, `NonInjective` isn’t injective, because it maps different
arguments to the same return value:

```
use typewit::{CallFn, RevTypeFn, TypeFn, UncallFn};

let _: CallFn<NonInjective, Vec<u8>> = 3u8;
let _: CallFn<NonInjective, String> = 5u8;

let _: UncallFn<NonInjective, u8> = ();

struct NonInjective;

impl<T> TypeFn<T> for NonInjective {
    type Output = u8;
}

impl RevTypeFn<u8> for NonInjective {
    type Arg = ();
}
```

# TypeNe in typewit - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/typewit/1.15.2/typewit/struct.TypeNe.html

## Expand description

Value-level proof that `L` is a different type to `R`

The opposite of [ TypeEq](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeEq.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use typewit::{const_marker::Usize, TypeNe};

assert_eq!(
    array_ref_chunks(&[3, 5, 8, 13, 21, 34, 55], AssertNotZero::V),
    Chunks {chunks: vec![&[3, 5, 8], &[13, 21, 34]], tail: &[55]}
);

fn array_ref_chunks<T, const LEN: usize>(
    slice: &[T],
    _not_zero: TypeNe<Usize<LEN>, Usize<0>>,
) -> Chunks<'_, T, LEN> {
    let mut chunks = slice.chunks_exact(LEN);

    Chunks {
        chunks: chunks.by_ref().map(|c| <&[T; LEN]>::try_from(c).unwrap()).collect(),
        tail: chunks.remainder(),
    }
}

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
struct Chunks<'a, T, const LEN: usize> {
    chunks: Vec<&'a [T; LEN]>,
    tail: &'a [T],
}

struct AssertNotZero<const N: usize>;

impl<const N: usize> AssertNotZero<N> {
    const V: TypeNe<Usize<N>, Usize<0>> = Usize::<N>.equals(Usize::<0>).unwrap_ne();
}

```
If you attempt to pass `0` as the length of the array chunks,
you’ll get this compile-time error:

```

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Constructs a `TypeNe` by mapping from a
`TypeNe<``LeftArg``, ``RightArg``>`
with an [injective type-level function](https://docs.rs/type_fn/trait.InjTypeFn.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#alternative)Alternative

The [ type_ne](https://docs.rs/macro.type_ne.html) macro can be used as syntactic sugar
for calling this constructor with a one-off type-level function.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use typewit::type_ne::{TypeNe, LeftArg, RightArg};

const NE: TypeNe<Option<String>, Vec<u16>> = TypeNe::with_fn(MakeNe::NEW);

typewit::inj_type_fn! {
    struct MakeNe<T, U>;

    impl LeftArg => Option<T>;
    impl RightArg => Vec<U>;
}
```
Joins a proof of `L != R` with a proof of `J == L`,
creating a proof of `J != R`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-5)Example

```
use typewit::{TypeEq, TypeNe, type_ne};

const NE: TypeNe<str, [u8]> = type_ne!(str, [u8]);

const fn foo<A: ?Sized>(eq: TypeEq<A, str>) {
    let _ne: TypeNe<A, [u8]> = NE.join_left(eq);
}
```
Joins a proof of `L != R` with a proof of `R == J`,
creating a proof of `L != J`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-6)Example

```
use typewit::{TypeEq, TypeNe, type_ne};

const NE: TypeNe<String, Vec<u8>> = type_ne!(String, Vec<u8>);

const fn foo<A>(eq: TypeEq<Vec<u8>, A>) {
    let _ne: TypeNe<String, A> = NE.join_right(eq);
}
```

**crate feature**only.

`rust_1_61`Combines this `TypeNe<L, R>` with an
[ A: BaseTypeWitness](https://docs.rs/trait.BaseTypeWitness.html) to produce a

`TypeNe<(L, A::L), (R, A::R)>`.[§](https://docs.rs#example-7)Example

```
use typewit::{TypeCmp, TypeEq, TypeNe, type_ne};

const NE: TypeNe<u8, i8> = type_ne!(u8, i8);
const EQ: TypeEq<u16, u16> = TypeEq::NEW;
const TC: TypeCmp<u32, u64> = TypeCmp::Ne(type_ne!(u32, u64));

let _: TypeNe<(u8, i8), (i8, u8)> = NE.zip(NE.flip());
let _: TypeNe<(u8, u16), (i8, u16)> = NE.zip(EQ);
let _: TypeNe<(u8, u32), (i8, u64)> = NE.zip(TC);

```

```
use typewit::{TypeCmp, TypeEq, TypeNe, type_ne};

const NE: TypeNe<u8, i8> = type_ne!(u8, i8);

let _: TypeNe<(u8, i8, u8), (i8, u8, i8)> = NE.zip3(NE.flip(), NE);
let _: TypeNe<(u8, u16, u16), (i8, u16, u16)> = NE.zip3(EQ, EQ.flip());
let _: TypeNe<(u8, u32, u64), (i8, u64, u32)> = NE.zip3(TC, TC.flip());

```

const NE: TypeNe<u8, i8> = type_ne!(u8, i8);
const EQ: TypeEq<u16, u16> = TypeEq::NEW;
const TC: TypeCmp<u32, u64> = TypeCmp::Ne(type_ne!(u32, u64));

let _: TypeNe<(u8, i8, u8, i8), (i8, u8, i8, u8)> = NE.zip4(NE.flip(), NE, NE.flip());
let _: TypeNe<(u8, u16, u16, u16), (i8, u16, u16, u16)> = NE.zip4(EQ, EQ.flip(), EQ);
let _: TypeNe<(u8, u32, u64, u32), (i8, u64, u32, u64)> = NE.zip4(TC, TC.flip(), TC);

```

#### pub const fn [map_to_arg](https://docs.rs#method.map_to_arg)<F, LA, RA>(
    self: [TypeNe](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeNe.html)<L, R>,
    func: F,
) -> [TypeNe](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeNe.html)<LA, RA>

#### pub const fn [map_to_arg](https://docs.rs#method.map_to_arg)<F, LA, RA>(
    self: [TypeNe](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeNe.html)<L, R>,
    func: F,
) -> [TypeNe](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeNe.html)<LA, RA>

Maps the `L` and `R` arguments of this `TypeNe<L, R>`
back to any argument of the `F` type-level function that would produce them.

Use this function over [ project_to_arg](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeNe.html#method.project_to_arg)
if you want the type of the passed in function to be inferred.

This operation is possible because `Call<F, LA> !=  Call<F, RA>` implies `LA != RA`,
i.e.: the return values being different implies that the arguments are different.

As opposed to [ unmap](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeNe.html#method.unmap),
this only requires

`F` to implement [, and the return type is determined by the caller.](https://docs.rs/type_fn/trait.TypeFn.html)

`TypeFn`[§](https://docs.rs#example-14)Example

Projecting from item type to collections

```
use typewit::TypeNe;

use std::ops::{Range, RangeInclusive};

with_typene(typewit::type_ne!(u8, i8));

const fn with_typene(ne: TypeNe<u8, i8>) {
    let _: TypeNe<Vec<u8>, [i8; 1]> = ne.map_to_arg(IntoIterFn);
    let _: TypeNe<Option<u8>, Result<i8, ()>> = ne.map_to_arg(IntoIterFn);
    let _: TypeNe<Range<u8>, RangeInclusive<i8>> = ne.map_to_arg(IntoIterFn);
}

typewit::type_fn!{
    struct IntoIterFn;

    impl<I: IntoIterator> I => I::Item
}
```

# TypeCmp in typewit - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/typewit/1.15.2/typewit/enum.TypeCmp.html

## Expand description

A witness of whether its `L` and `R` type parameters are the same or different types.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[§](https://docs.rs#custom-array-creation)Custom array creation

(this example requires Rust 1.63.0, because of [ core::array::from_fn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/array/fn.from_fn.html)).

```
use typewit::{const_marker::Usize, TypeCmp, TypeEq, TypeNe};

let empty: [String; 0] = [];
assert_eq!(ArrayMaker::<String, 0>::empty().make(), empty);

assert_eq!(ArrayMaker::<u8, 2>::defaulted().make(), [0u8, 0u8]);

assert_eq!(ArrayMaker::with(|i| i.pow(2)).make(), [0usize, 1, 4, 9]);

enum ArrayMaker<T, const LEN: usize> {
    NonEmpty(fn(usize) -> T, TypeNe<[T; LEN], [T; 0]>),
    Empty(TypeEq<[T; LEN], [T; 0]>),
}

impl<T, const LEN: usize> ArrayMaker<T, LEN> {
    pub fn make(self) -> [T; LEN] {
        match self {
            ArrayMaker::NonEmpty(func, _) => std::array::from_fn(func),
            ArrayMaker::Empty(te) => te.to_left([]),
        }
    }

    pub const fn defaulted() -> Self
    where
        T: Default
    {
        Self::with(|_| Default::default())
    }

    pub const fn with(func: fn(usize) -> T) -> Self {
        match  Usize::<LEN>.equals(Usize::<0>) // : TypeCmp<Usize<LEN>, Usize<0>>
            .project::<ArrayFn<T>>() // : TypeCmp<[T; LEN], [T; 0]>
        {
            TypeCmp::Ne(ne) => ArrayMaker::NonEmpty(func, ne),
            TypeCmp::Eq(eq) => ArrayMaker::Empty(eq),
        }
    }
}

impl<T> ArrayMaker<T, 0> {
    pub const fn empty() -> Self {
        Self::Empty(TypeEq::NEW)
    }
}

impl<T, const LEN: usize> Copy for ArrayMaker<T, LEN> {}

impl<T, const LEN: usize> Clone for ArrayMaker<T, LEN> {
    fn clone(&self) -> Self { *self }
}

typewit::inj_type_fn! {
    // Declares `struct ArrayFn`, which implements `InjTypeFn<Usize<LEN>>`:
    // an injective type-level function from `Usize<LEN>` to `[T; LEN]`
    struct ArrayFn<T>;
    impl<const LEN: usize> Usize<LEN> => [T; LEN]
}
```

Constructs a `TypeCmp<L, R>` by comparing the `L` and `R` types for equality.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use typewit::TypeCmp;

let eq: TypeCmp<u8, u8> = TypeCmp::with_any();
assert!(matches!(eq, TypeCmp::Eq(_)));

let ne = TypeCmp::<u8, i8>::with_any();
assert!(matches!(ne, TypeCmp::Ne(_)));
```

    TC_EQ.zip(NE),

    TC_EQ.zip(EQ),
    TypeCmp::<(i64, u16), (i64, u16)>::Eq(_),
));

assert!(matches!(
    TC_EQ.zip(TC_EQ),
    TypeCmp::<(i64, i64), (i64, i64)>::Eq(_),

    TC_EQ.zip(TC_NE),
    TypeCmp::<(i64, u32), (i64, u64)>::Ne(_),

This returns either [ TypeCmp::Eq](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeCmp.html#variant.Eq) or

[depending on the arguments:](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeCmp.html#variant.Ne)

`TypeCmp::Ne`- if all arguments (including `self`) are`TypeEq``TypeCmp::Eq``TypeCmp::Eq`
- if any argument (including `self`) is a`TypeNe``TypeCmp::Ne``TypeCmp::Ne`

[§](https://docs.rs#example-15)Example

```
use typewit::{TypeCmp, TypeEq, TypeNe, type_ne};

const NE: TypeNe<u8, i8> = type_ne!(u8, i8);
const EQ: TypeEq<u16, u16> = TypeEq::NEW;
const TC_NE: TypeCmp<u32, u64> = TypeCmp::Ne(type_ne!(u32, u64));
const TC_EQ: TypeCmp<i64, i64> = TypeCmp::Eq(TypeEq::NEW);

assert!(matches!(
    TC_EQ.zip4(EQ, NE, TC_NE),
    TypeCmp::<(i64, u16, u8, u32), (i64, u16, i8, u64)>::Ne(_),
));

assert!(matches!(
    TC_EQ.zip4(EQ, TC_EQ, EQ),
    TypeCmp::<(i64, u16, i64, u16), (i64, u16, i64, u16)>::Eq(_),
));
```
Maps the type arguments of this `TypeCmp`
by using the `F` [injective type-level function](https://docs.rs/type_fn/trait.InjTypeFn.html).

Use this function over [ project](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeCmp.html#method.project)
if you want the type of the passed in function to be inferred.

inj_type_fn!{
    struct WrappingFn;

    impl<T> T => Wrapping<T>

`O:``BaseTypeWitness``<L = Usize<UL>, R = Usize<UR>>`

[§](https://docs.rs#alternative-3)Alternative

[ methods::in_array](https://docs.rs/methods/fn.in_array.html)

This method always returns `TypeCmp`,
while [that function](https://docs.rs/methods/fn.in_array.html)

`TypeNe`.[§](https://docs.rs#returned-variant-3)Returned variant

This returns either [ TypeCmp::Eq](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeCmp.html#variant.Eq) or

[depending on the arguments:](https://docs.rs/enum.TypeCmp.html#variant.Ne)

`TypeCmp::Ne`- if all arguments (including `self`) are`TypeEq``TypeCmp::Eq``TypeCmp::Eq`
- if any argument (including `self`) is a`TypeNe``TypeCmp::Ne``TypeCmp::Ne`

[§](https://docs.rs#example-23)Example

[§](https://docs.rs#basic)Basic

```
use typewit::{
    const_marker::Usize,
    TypeCmp, TypeEq, TypeNe,
    type_ne,
};

let cmp_eq_ty: TypeCmp<i32, i32> = TypeCmp::Eq(TypeEq::NEW);
let cmp_ne_ty: TypeCmp<i64, u64> = TypeCmp::Ne(type_ne!(i64, u64));

let eq_len: TypeEq<Usize<0>, Usize<0>> = TypeEq::NEW;
let ne_len: TypeNe<Usize<1>, Usize<2>> = Usize.equals(Usize).unwrap_ne();
let cmp_eq_len: TypeCmp<Usize<3>, Usize<3>> = Usize.equals(Usize);
let cmp_ne_len: TypeCmp<Usize<5>, Usize<8>> = Usize.equals(Usize);

assert!(matches!(cmp_eq_ty.in_array(eq_len), TypeCmp::<[i32; 0], [i32; 0]>::Eq(_)));
assert!(matches!(cmp_eq_ty.in_array(ne_len), TypeCmp::<[i32; 1], [i32; 2]>::Ne(_)));
assert!(matches!(cmp_eq_ty.in_array(cmp_eq_len), TypeCmp::<[i32; 3], [i32; 3]>::Eq(_)));
assert!(matches!(cmp_eq_ty.in_array(cmp_ne_len), TypeCmp::<[i32; 5], [i32; 8]>::Ne(_)));

assert!(matches!(cmp_ne_ty.in_array(eq_len), TypeCmp::<[i64; 0], [u64; 0]>::Ne(_)));
assert!(matches!(cmp_ne_ty.in_array(ne_len), TypeCmp::<[i64; 1], [u64; 2]>::Ne(_)));
assert!(matches!(cmp_ne_ty.in_array(cmp_eq_len), TypeCmp::<[i64; 3], [u64; 3]>::Ne(_)));
assert!(matches!(cmp_ne_ty.in_array(cmp_ne_len), TypeCmp::<[i64; 5], [u64; 8]>::Ne(_)));
```

# typewit::type_fn - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/typewit/1.15.2/typewit/type_fn/index.html

## Expand description

Type-level functions.

Type-level functions come in two flavors:
[injective](https://docs.rs#injective), and [non-injective](https://docs.rs#non-injective)

[§](https://docs.rs#injective)Injective

An injective function is any function `f` for which `a != b` implies `f(a) != f(b)`.

(For both injective and non-injective functions, `f(a) != f(b)` implies `a != b`)

The [ InjTypeFn](https://docs.rs/trait.InjTypeFn.html) trait encodes injective type-level functions,
requiring the type to implement both

[and](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeFn.html)

`TypeFn`[.](https://docs.rs/trait.RevTypeFn.html)

`RevTypeFn`[§](https://docs.rs#example-injective-function)Example: injective function

```
typewit::inj_type_fn!{
    struct Upcast;

    impl u8 => u16;
    impl u16 => u32;
    impl u32 => u64;
    impl u64 => u128;
}
let _: CallInjFn<Upcast, u8> = 3u16;
let _: CallInjFn<Upcast, u16> = 5u32;
```
Because `Upcast` is injective,
it is possible to query the argument from the returned value:

```
let _: UncallFn<Upcast, u16> = 3u8;
let _: UncallFn<Upcast, u128> = 5u64;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-injective)Non-injective

The [ TypeFn](https://docs.rs/trait.TypeFn.html) trait allows implementors to be non-injective.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-non-injective-function)Example: non-injective function

```
typewit::type_fn!{
    struct Bar;

    impl<T> Vec<T> => T;
    impl<T> Box<T> => T;
}
```
`Bar` is *non*-injective because it maps both `Vec<T>` and `Box<T>` to `T`.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::`- [inj_type_fn](https://docs.rs/macro.inj_type_fn.html);
- `pub use crate::`- [type_fn](https://docs.rs/index.html);
- `pub use crate::`- [type_fn](https://docs.rs/macro.type_fn.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [FnIdentity](https://docs.rs/struct.FnIdentity.html)
- Type-level identity function
- [FnRev](https://docs.rs/struct.FnRev.html)
- Reverses an `InjTypeFn`
- [GBox](https://docs.rs/struct.GBox.html)- `alloc`
- Type-level function from `T`to`Box<T>`
- [GRef](https://docs.rs/struct.GRef.html)
- Type-level function from `T`to`&'a T`
- [GRefMut](https://docs.rs/struct.GRefMut.html)
- Type-level function from `T`to`&'a mut T`
- [Invoke](https://docs.rs/struct.Invoke.html)
- Type-level function which implements `TypeFn`by delegating to`F`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- An  [injective](https://docs.rs/index.html#injective)type-level function
- [RevType](https://docs.rs/trait.RevTypeFn.html)- Fn
- The inverse of `TypeFn``TypeFn`

# inj_type_fn in typewit - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/typewit/1.15.2/typewit/macro.inj_type_fn.html

```
macro_rules! inj_type_fn {
    ($($args:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
## Expand description

Declares an
[injective type-level function](https://docs.rs/type_fn/trait.InjTypeFn.html)

This macro takes in the exact same syntax as the [ type_fn](https://docs.rs/macro.type_fn.html) macro.

This macro generates the same items as the `type_fn` macro,
in addition to implementing [ RevTypeFn](https://docs.rs/type_fn/trait.RevTypeFn.html),
so that the function implements

[.](https://docs.rs/type_fn/trait.InjTypeFn.html)

`InjTypeFn`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

This macro is also demonstrated in
`TypeNe::{``map``, ``project``, ``unmap``, ``unproject``}`.

[§](https://docs.rs#basic)Basic

```
use typewit::{CallFn, UncallFn, inj_type_fn};

// Calls the `ToSigned` function with `u64` as the argument.
let _: CallFn<ToSigned, u64> = 3i64;

// Gets the argument of the `ToSigned` function from the `i8` return value.
let _: UncallFn<ToSigned, i8> = 5u8;

inj_type_fn!{
    struct ToSigned;

    impl u128 => i128;
    impl u64 => i64;
    impl u32 => i32;
    impl u16 => i16;
    impl u8 => i8;
}
```
##

struct ToSigned;

impl ToSigned {

impl ::typewit::TypeFn<u128> for ToSigned {
    type Output = i128;
}

impl ::typewit::RevTypeFn<i128> for ToSigned {
    type Arg = u128;
}

impl ::typewit::TypeFn<u64> for ToSigned {
    type Output = i64;
}

impl ::typewit::RevTypeFn<i64> for ToSigned {
    type Arg = u64;
}

impl ::typewit::TypeFn<u32> for ToSigned {
    type Output = i32;

impl ::typewit::RevTypeFn<i32> for ToSigned {
    type Arg = u32;
}

impl ::typewit::TypeFn<u16> for ToSigned {

impl ::typewit::RevTypeFn<i16> for ToSigned {
    type Arg = u16;
}

impl ::typewit::TypeFn<u8> for ToSigned {
